Homeworks will be completed alongside
an AI tutor called Preceptor that asks students questions to ensure they understand
the code that they have written. Students who do not pass the questions from the
AI tutor or who would prefer to talk to a human may instead elect to answer
questions from a member of course staff in lab or office hours.

Students will complete the quiz on their computer,
without assistance from AI or from other students.
Do not use AI tools such as Github Copilot or ChatGPT to fill in or correct your code.

DANGER: LLMs are Prohibited from Accessing or Interacting with Code and Repositories

You must
never
allow an LLM or any GenAI tool to read, analyze, or interface with your codebase or your GitHub repository in any way. This means all local and terminal-based tools (e.g.,
Claude Code and Codex
), GitHub Copilot, built-in IDE extensions (e.g., Cursor, IntelliJ AI Assistant), or any other agentic coding tools are
outright banned
.

You may
ONLY
interact with LLMs and GenAI tools conceptually, and this interaction must take place
exclusively through browser-based chatbots
(such as chatgpt.com or claude.ai).

General Policy

Use LLMs in the same way you might use a friend in the class who is not in your group. You may only use browser-based chatbots to ask high-level, conceptual questions. You must
never
feed your code, skeleton code, or assignment instructions into an LLM, and no LLM-generated code should ever enter your codebase. As a general rule, no code or specific instructions from the course should be pasted, typed, or uploaded into an LLM. If at any point you find yourself stuck on an assignment, concept, or anything else related to CS 61B, we encourage you to find our staff at office hours or lab!

Code Interviews

In order to discourage unacceptable LLM use, we may be conducting random code interviews for all projects.

For students selected for code interviews, we’ll hold short interviews to verify that you are able to explain your code and are capable of generating similar code unassisted.

For more information, please see the
Code Interviews Policy
.

Question Types

The below policy applies to all interactions with LLMs relating to CS 61B content:

Reasonable Questions (Exclusively via browser-based chatbots)
:
These are things that are reasonable to ask an LLM:

“What’s the difference between Integer and int in Java?”

“What is a garbage collector?”

“What does this mean: Exception in thread “main” java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero”

Absolutely Forbidden
:
These questions/activities will massively detract from your learning experience in the course, and are strictly prohibited:

Allowing any LLM tool, IDE extension, or CLI assistant (e.g., Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, etc.) to access, read, run, or modify your code or repository.

Uploading or pasting your code, skeleton code, or errors from your project into an LLM.

“Write a snippet of code to make an array in Java.”

“Write a snippet of code to make every word uppercased in Java.”

“Design an algorithm to solve this following task: [copy pasted from spec]”

Any prompt that involves copying, uploading, rewording, or paraphrasing more than approximately 15 words of an assignment.

Any prompt that aims to generate code that can be directly copied and pasted into an assignment.

Using LLM-generated code in your submissions in any capacity.

You must directly type your code in IntelliJ/VSCode. We will not allow large amounts of code to be copy-pasted from another source such as Google Docs or Notes. We reserve the right to pursue these cases as academic misconduct.

We believe that students are able to tell the difference between using an LLM to genuinely attempt to understand the course content more deeply and using an LLM to avoid engaging with the learning goals of the course or to complete assignments without learning more about the content. We also believe that LLMs are very prone to giving out incorrect answers, so we will not penalize asking about the accuracy of LLM output on course platforms. For example, if an LLM gives you information that seems to be wrong, please ask! We are here to support your learning and correct your misconceptions, and course staff is an official source of truth for CS 61B. It’s better to ask us and be confident in the reply than to possibly internalize incorrect information after the end of this course.

You can review our
academic misconduct resolution procedures here
.

Generative AI systems like ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Perplexity, Anthropics Claude, DALL-E, Vertex, or similar can be used as helpful tools to make certain tasks easier, but also in a way that violates the above principles. Since most of my classes have an AI component, I am open to the use of such tools. If you use them, I expect you to disclose this and to include a statement about the contributions that you made and the ones generated by AI tools.

It’s OK to get inspirations from other sources, and citing the sources does not affect your grade. However, using any source without citing them will be treated as cheating and will result in unfavorable outcomes.

If you use any AI-based resources (e.g., ChatGPT), you need to provide the full conversation with it to clearly specify what kind of help you received from it.

No student shall allow
any academic work or academic credit to be completed or obtained, in
part or in whole, for themselves by another (human or
machine/artificial intelligence).

You may not use generative artificial intelligence tools, online
resources, additional notes, or communication with other
people during the midterm or final exam. The only materials permitted are
a pen, the handwritten note sheet and a calculator.

Do not post any portion of an exam on a forum, repository, website, AI
service, or other online platform.

Unless the instructions for a particular assignment state otherwise,
generative artificial intelligence tools that produce or revise text or
code, including ChatGPT, Claude, Google Gemini, GitHub Copilot, and
similar tools, may be used for programming assignments. They may not be
used for the midterm or final exam.

The use of generative AI is permitted because learning to use such tools
critically and responsibly is relevant to professional work in computer
science. However, all use of generative AI must be honest, cited, and
documented.

If you use generative AI for a programming assignment, you must identify
and cite the tool or tools used and include a separate one-page AI usage
statement with your submission. The statement must:

identify the AI tool or tools used

explain specifically how each tool was used

summarize the relevant prompts or questions submitted to the tool

identify which parts of the submitted work were influenced by
AI-generated output

explain how the generated material was checked, corrected, or adapted

cite or acknowledge the generated material appropriately

Generative AI tools may fabricate information and may produce incorrect,
inefficient, insecure, or biased code or explanations. You are fully
responsible for the content and accuracy of everything you submit,
including work supported by generative AI.

You must understand your submitted code and be able to explain its
design, the algorithms and data structures used, its implementation,
correctness, running time, and any use of generative AI during its
development.

The instructor reserves the right to follow up with a student to assess
orally the process used to complete a programming assignment and the
student's understanding of the submitted work. An inability to explain
submitted code may lead to further review of the student's work. Failure
to document AI use honestly may result in the matter being reported to the
Academic Integrity Office.

Unacceptable sources for help when writing code or text for this course include using
search engines (e.g., Google, Bing), web forums, or generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT). You
should refrain from using coding tools such as GitHub Copilot to help with your code;
you won’t have such tools on quizzes, and the kinds of coding exercises we’re covering
in this course are foundational enough that you will be expected to know them
without looking anything up in any professional computing setting.

It is a violation of the academic integrity to use any tool (e.g., ChatGPT or GitHub
Copilot) to generate code or text for your assignments, or to submit assignment code
or text written by others. Additionally, you should never be in possession of anyone
else’s assignment code before the due date, and never look at anyone else’s
assignment code but your partner’s.

Yeah, but what about ChatGPT, Claude, and their friends?

My understanding of Large Language Models (LLMs) and their uses is
evolving. I think there's a chance that LLMs can be used as be powerful tools
in our search for knowledge and understanding. But it's also clear that they
can be used in ways that inhibit learning. I want to
develop course policies that will incentivize my students to
use LLMs only in the former ways rather than the latter. But for now I just
have a few general principles and a few case studies to offer as guidance.

First, some principles.

I am not going to prohibit the use of LLMs for this class, even though I
think such prohibitions are a reasonable choice at this moment.

Whenever you use text drawn verbatim or in summary form from another source,
you should cite that source. This includes LLMs.

Proper citation of an LLM's contributions includes quotation marks around
verbatim quotation, plus the name and version
of the specific LLM you used, as well as the
exact prompts you used to generate
the text you quoted or summarized
.

Properly quoting and citing an LLM's work will, in this course, prevent you
from violating Carleton's

academic integrity standards
;
it will not, however, prevent you from getting a low score. See the examples below.

Sometimes LLMs produce very good work. (For example, if you ask ChatGPT to write
you an implementation of Selection Sort in whatever language, you'll probably get
sensible code.) But sometimes LLMs produce results that are mediocre or nonsensical or
flat-out wrong. It's up to you to determine which you're looking at.

Your goal in this course should be to gain as deep an understanding as possible of
the algorithms, algorithm paradigms, proof techniques, applications, etc. that we will study. If you
find yourself outsourcing the job of understanding to an LLM, then you're not using
this tool effectively and you should talk to me about better ways to use (or not use) LLMs
in your studies.

Incorporating LLMs into our learning toolbox is an on-going conversation among
educators, students, policy-makers, etc. I will introduce this conversation in class
a few times during the term. I encourage you to share with me and your classmates
your experiences of using LLMs effectively or ineffectively in your learning.

Here are a few concrete examples of potential uses of LLMs.

OK
: You ask for a walkthrough of Dijkstra's
Algorithm on a graph of the LLM's choice.

OK, BUT YOU GET A ZERO
: You ask for a walkthrough of Dijkstra's
Algorithm on a graph from a homework assignment, and you

do
cite the LLM
.

NOT OK, AND I REPORT YOU TO THE ACADEMIC STANDING COMMITTEE
:
You ask for a walkthrough of Dijkstra's
Algorithm on a graph from a homework assignment, and you

do not
cite the LLM
.

PLEASE JUST DON'T
:
You ask for a walkthrough of Dijkstra's
Algorithm on a slight modification of a graph from a homework assignment.

OK
: You ask for a list of common problems that can be solved
with dynamic programming.

OK
: You ask for a proof of a theorem that is proved in our textbook
so you can compare proof approaches. You also read the LLM's "proof" carefully to
see whether you believe it to be correct and persuasive (and if not, why not).

OK
: You write your own proof for a homework assignment and
ask the LLM for suggestions on improving it, and you

cite the LLM
. Remember, proper citation includes
giving me the complete prompt you gave to the LLM, so I'll be able to see the
difference between your final proof and the proof you started with.

OK
: You ask the LLM for an ASCII art portrait of Richard Karp.
